O you who have believed, when you meet those who have disbelieved advancing (zahfan), do not turn your backs to them (fa-la tuwallawhum al-adbar).

That is, "advancing" means approaching one another in battle (mutazahifin). Al-tazahuf (mutual advance) is drawing near for fighting, and its meaning is: when you advance upon one another and meet in battle. "Do not turn your backs to them" means: do not flee, for the one who flees turns his back when he runs away.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 16:

﴿And whoever turns his back to them on that day, unless he is swerving to (engage in) battle﴾ Al-taharruf lil-qital (swerving for battle) is when one shows retreat while intending by it to seek an opening, a surprise attack, and to seize the opportunity. ﴿Or retreating to a company﴾ meaning: inclining toward a company. ﴿Then he has returned with anger from Allah﴾ meaning: he has returned with anger from Allah. ﴿And his refuge is Hell, and wretched is the destination.﴾ The Mu'tazilah took as evidence the unrestricted wording of His saying: ﴿And his refuge is Hell﴾ as a threat of eternal punishment. But they have no proof in it, because the meaning of the verse is: "And his refuge is Hell," unless the mercy reaches him; this is shown by the other verses that restrict it.

Al-Hasan al-Basri said: the verse refers specifically to the people of Badr. It was not permissible for them to flee under any circumstances, because the Prophet was with them and they had no company to which they could withdraw. As for others, fleeing from the battle is not a major sin, because the Muslims are a company for one another, so the fleeing person is withdrawing to a company.

This is narrated from Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, one of the Companions, and the statement of Umar, may Allah be pleased with him, supports this: when the Muslims were struck at the Day of the Bridge with what struck them and they endured until they were killed, Umar said: "Why did they not return to me?" And whenever he sent an army after that, he would say: "I am a company for every Muslim."

It is also supported by what is narrated from Ibn Umar, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: "We undertook a raid, and we were routed in disarray, so we said: 'O Messenger of Allah, are we the fleeing ones?' He said: 'No; rather you are the ones who regroup, and I am your company.'"

There is another opinion regarding the verse, which is the prevailing position today and the view of the majority of jurists: if the disbelievers are more than twice the number of the Muslims, fleeing from the battle is permissible, based on His saying: ﴿Now Allah has lightened for you﴾ and His saying: ﴿And do not throw yourselves with your own hands into destruction﴾. And if they endure, it is permissible, unless they know with certainty that they cannot withstand them; then endurance is not permissible, because it would be casting oneself into destruction. And if the disbelievers are equal to the Muslims or fewer than twice their number, fleeing from the battle is not permissible except by swerving to battle or retreating to a company — meaning, to a company near the army, such as the detachments (sarayā). And fleeing from the battle occurs mostly in this form.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 17:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿So you did not kill them, but it was Allah who killed them﴾. The occasion of this was that when the Muslims returned from the battle of Badr, one of them would say, "I killed so-and-so," and another would say, "I killed so-and-so." Allah, exalted is He, was not pleased with them for this, and the verse was revealed: ﴿So you did not kill them﴾, meaning: by your own strength and your numbers, ﴿but it was Allah who killed them﴾ (by His help) — by His aid to you and His support of you. It has also been said that its meaning is: but Allah killed them by driving them towards you until you gained victory over them.

It has also been said that its meaning is: but Allah killed them by sending the angels to you as reinforcements, so Allah killed them through the angels.

﴿And you did not throw when you threw, but Allah threw﴾. It is related that the Prophet (ﷺ) took a handful of pebbles on the day of Badr, threw them towards the faces of the polytheists, and said, "May the faces be disfigured." Not one of them remained without some of it reaching his eyes, and they were occupied with their eyes.

By ﴿And you did not throw when you threw﴾ he means that throwing of the pebbles which reached their eyes, since this is not within the capacity of human beings: to throw pebbles at the faces of an army such that no eye is left without being struck by them. ﴿But Allah threw﴾ by His might and power. It has also been said that its meaning is: "And you did not reach when you threw; but Allah reached." It has also been said that its meaning is: "And you did not cast terror into their hearts; but Allah did."

﴿And that He might bestow upon the believers a fine favour from Him﴾. That is, a good blessing which He bestows upon the believers, and this blessing is the gift of victory and triumph. Hardship is a trial, and blessing is a trial, and Allah tests His servant sometimes with blessing and sometimes with hardship. ﴿Indeed Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾.

Al-Sam'ani's commentary on Surah 8, verse 18:

God's words: ﴿That is so, and that God weakens the plotting of the disbelievers﴾ are read both with a light (mukhaffaf) and a doubled (mushaddad) form of the verb, and its meaning is: He weakens the plotting of the disbelievers.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 19:

His saying: ﴿If you seek a victory, then the victory has certainly come to you﴾. Al-Dahhak said: The cause of this was that Abu Jahl said on the day of Badr: "O Allah, give victory to the one of the two groups that is dearer to You and more honoured in Your sight." In another narration: "O Allah, sever ties of kinship with us, break up our community, and bring us that which we do not recognise; so destroy him today." Allah, exalted is He, answered him with His saying: ﴿If you seek a victory﴾, meaning: if you seek help, then help has certainly come to you.

﴿And if you desist, it is better for you; and if you return, We will return; and your company will not avail you anything, though it be numerous; and that Allah is with the believers﴾.

Almost there: the passage is short, so translating directly.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿O you who have believed, obey Allah and His Messenger﴾. He commands the Companions to obey Him and to obey His Messenger. ﴿And do not turn away from him﴾, meaning: do not turn away from him. {While you hear}.
﴿Do not be like those who said, "We hear," while they do not hear.﴾ He means: since they did not benefit from what they heard, it is as if they had not heard. So do not be like them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 22:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah are the deaf and the dumb who do not use reason﴾. He named the disbelievers "deaf and dumb" because, when they did not hear the truth, did not speak the truth, and did not understand the truth, He named them thus and counted them among the cattle (al-an'am).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 23:

﴿And if Allah had known any good in them, He would have made them hear.﴾ That is: He would have made them hear with the hearing of understanding and acceptance, if He had known that they were fit for that.

﴿And if He had made them hear, they would have turned away while they were averse.﴾ If it is asked: how is His saying consistent, ﴿He would have made them hear﴾ and ﴿if He had made them hear they would have turned away﴾? It is said: its meaning is that if He had known any good in them He would have made them hear with the hearing of understanding, and if He had made them hear with the hearing of the ears they would have turned away. It is also said: its meaning is that if He had made them hear with the hearing of understanding they would have turned away, because of the wretchedness that had preceded for them, and because they were not fit for that and there was no good in them. It is also said: its meaning is that they used to say to the Prophet: "Revive Qusayy for us, for he was a blessed old man, so that we may bear witness to you regarding prophethood and believe in you." So Allah the Exalted said: ﴿And if He had made them hear﴾ the speech of Qusayy ﴿they would have turned away while they were averse.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 24:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿O you who have believed, respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life﴾. As-Suddi said concerning His saying ﴿that which gives you life﴾: He meant by it faith (iman). As-Suddi was given that name because he used to sit at the doorway (sudda) of the mosque of Kufa.

Qatadah said: it is the Qur'an. Al-Farra' said: it is jihad. Ibn Qutaybah said: it is martyrdom (shahadah).

Abu Hurayrah narrated that the Prophet called Ubayy ibn Ka'b while he was in prayer, so he quickened his recitation, completed the prayer, and then answered him. The Prophet said: "What prevented you from answering me?" He said: "I was in prayer." He (peace be upon him) said: "Did you not hear the saying of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Respond to Allah and to the Messenger when he calls you to that which gives you life﴾?" He said: "I understood, and I will not do it again."

﴿And know that Allah comes between a person and his heart﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr and a group said: He comes between the believer and disbelief, and between the disbeliever and faith. Ad-Dahhak said: He comes between the believer and disobedience, and between the disbeliever and obedience.

There is a third opinion: its meaning is that He comes between the believer and fear, and between the disbeliever and security; this is because the disbelievers were secure while the Muslims were fearful, so Allah, exalted is He, exchanged the fear of these with security and the security of those with fear. He expressed it with "the heart" because it is the seat of fear and security. ﴿And that to Him you will be gathered﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 25:

The words of God Most High: ﴿And beware of a trial which will not afflict those among you who have done wrong in particular﴾. The majority of the exegetes (mufassirun) hold that the verse concerns the companions of the Prophet, and its meaning is: beware of a punishment that strikes both the wrongdoer and the one who is not a wrongdoer.

Al-Zubayr, when he saw what he saw on the day of the Camel, said: "I did not know that this verse was revealed concerning us, the companions of the Messenger of God, until this day."

Ibn 'Abbas said regarding the meaning of the verse: "Do not acknowledge the evil (al-munkar) among you, and enjoin the good (al-ma'ruf), lest God encompass you with a punishment that strikes both the wrongdoer and the one who is not a wrongdoer."

It has also been said: he meant by the trial (fitnah) the scattering of the word (tafriq al-kalimah) and the difference of opinions. "Beware of a trial, the scattering of the word, which will not afflict those among you who have done wrong in particular," so the punishment is implied in it. ﴿And know that God is severe in punishment﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 26:

The words of His Exalted saying: ﴿And remember when you were few and oppressed in the land, fearing that the people would snatch you away﴾. Wahb ibn Munabbih said: It means: Persia would snatch you away. ʿIkrimah said: The disbelieving Arabs would snatch you away. ﴿So He sheltered you﴾, meaning: to Madinah. ﴿And strengthened you with His help﴾, meaning: He strengthened you with His victory. ﴿And provided for you of the good things﴾, meaning: the spoils of war. ﴿That perhaps you may be grateful﴾.

O you who believe, do not betray God and the Messenger, nor betray your trusts while you know (better).

Al-Kalbi said: The verse was revealed concerning Abu Lubaba ibn 'Abd al-Mundhir. When the Prophet (ﷺ) besieged Banu Qurayza, he sent him to them, and he was one of them (an ally). They said to him: "What would he do to us if we came down under his judgment?" He placed his finger on his throat and gestured to them with the slaughter, meaning: he will kill you. Abu Lubaba said: "My feet had not moved from their place before I realized that I had betrayed God and His Messenger." And the verse was revealed.

It is also said: the verse concerns all trusts. It forbids the servants from betraying trusts. Acts of obedience (ta'at) are included among the trusts, since they are trusts held by the servants, in the sense that they are between them and their Lord, whether they fulfil them or do not fulfil them.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on Surah 8, verse 28:

The words of the Most High: ﴿And know that your wealth and your children are but a trial, and that with Allah is a great reward﴾. It was said: this too was revealed concerning Abu Lubaba, for his family, his children and his wealth were among them, so he said what he said out of fear for them. It was also said: it refers to all of creation. And in the hadith: "Children are a cause of cowardice, a cause of miserliness, and a cause of ignorance."

It is narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) saw al-Hasan and al-Husayn and said: "You make me cowardly, you make me miserly, and you make me ignorant, and you are indeed a fragrance (rayhan) of Allah." He pointed to al-Hasan and al-Husayn, meaning: you cause the fathers to fall into cowardice, miserliness and ignorance. And his saying "a fragrance of Allah" means: from the provision of Allah.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿O you who have believed, if you fear Allah, He will grant you a criterion (furqan), and will remove from you your misdeeds and forgive you. And Allah is the possessor of great bounty.﴾

Ibn 'Abbas said: "Furqan" means a way out (makhraj). Mujahid said: it means deliverance (manjah).

﴿And will remove from you your misdeeds and forgive you, and Allah is the possessor of great bounty.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 30:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [remember] when those who disbelieved plotted against you, to confine you, or kill you, or expel you﴾. The occasion of revelation of the verse is that the polytheists gathered in the Dar al-Nadwa (the assembly house of Quraysh) to deliberate about the matter of the Messenger of Allah. Iblis entered upon them in the form of an old man. They said to him: "What brought you in upon us?" He said: "I am an old man from Najd, and I am not from Tihama. It has reached me that you have gathered concerning the matter of this man, and that he will not lack an opinion from me." They said: "Leave him," then they consulted. 'Utba said: "Tie him on a camel and expel him from your land, and the Arabs will be rid of him for you." Iblis said: "This is not an opinion. Do you not see the sweetness of his speech and how it captivates hearts? If you did that to him, he would go and win over the hearts of a people, then attack you and split your gathering." So they abandoned that. Abu al-Bakhtari ibn Hisham said: "We imprison him in a house and wait for him to meet the fate of the dead (rayb al-manun)." Iblis said: "This is not an opinion, for he has a clan and a people who will not accept this and will expel him." So they abandoned that. Abu Jahl said: "I have an opinion: these are five clans of Quraysh. We choose from each clan a strong youth, and we place in his hand a sharp sword, and we order them to strike him in a single blow, so that his blood is scattered among the tribes, and his people will be unable to fight, and they will accept the blood-money." Iblis said: "This is the opinion," and they dispersed upon it. Then Allah, exalted is He, informed of their plotting, and the verse was revealed. It is related that the Prophet sent Abu Bakr to examine their condition. When he came to them, Iblis had come out from among them. He walked with him for a while, then when he wanted to part from him, Abu Bakr said to him: "Where are you going?" The accursed one said: "I have a people in this valley." Abu Bakr knew that he was Iblis, so he said: "Praise be to Allah who has disgraced you and made His religion manifest," and he vanished from him. So His saying ﴿And [remember] when those who disbelieved plotted against you﴾ refers to that plotting of theirs, and al-makr (plotting) is planning. ﴿To confine you﴾, that is, to imprison you, as Abu al-Bakhtari said. ﴿Or kill you﴾, as Abu Jahl said. ﴿Or expel you﴾, as 'Utba said.

﴿And they plot, and Allah plots﴾. The plotting from Allah is planning with truth; it has also been said that it is seizing suddenly. al-Zajjaj said its meaning is: He requites them with the recompense of plotting.

﴿And Allah is the best of the plotters﴾, that is, the best of the planners.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Qur'an) on surah 8, verse 31:

Allah's words: ﴿And when Our verses are recited to them, they say, "We have heard. If we wished, we could say the like of this."﴾ This is the statement of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith ibn Kaladah. He had gone out to al-Hira in the land of Iraq, bought the stories of Rustam and Isfandiyar and the tales of the non-Arabs (al-'Ajam), and brought them to Mecca, saying: "If I wished, I could say the like of the Qur'an." That is the meaning of His words: ﴿If we wished, we could say the like of this.﴾

﴿This is nothing but the tales of the ancients.﴾ That is, the lies of the ancients. Al-asatir (tales) is the plural of al-usturah (a legend, a fable), which means "that which is written down."

If it is said: When the Qur'an is inimitable (mu'jiz), how can His words ﴿If we wished, we could say the like of this﴾ be consistent? Would anyone say: "If I wished, I could turn stone into gold and a staff into a serpent," while being unable to do so?

It is said: The Qur'an is a lure that cannot be attained; some of its listeners may imagine that they can say the like of it, but this is impossible for them, and thus their assumption is mistaken. It is also said: he imagined, out of his ignorance, that he was able to produce the like of it, while in fact he was incapable.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 32:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And when they said, "O Allah, if this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment."﴾ Most of the exegetes hold that this was the statement of al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, but in the Sahih, on the authority of Anas, it is related that this was the statement of Abu Jahl, may the curse of Allah be upon him.

This indicates the extent of their obstinacy in disbelief, and that they had no doubt or suspicion regarding the Messenger's lying; for a sensible person does not ask for punishment in this manner while being uncertain about the matter. This is evidence that knowledge ('irfan) is not necessary (darurah) for one who knows.

It is related from Mu'awiyah that he said to a man from the people of Yemen: "How ignorant your people are, in that they said: 'Our Lord, make the distances between our journeys farther apart.'" The man replied: "And how much more ignorant are your people, in that they said: ﴿If this is indeed the truth from You, then rain down on us stones from the sky or bring us a painful punishment.﴾"

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 33:

His words, may He be exalted: ﴿But Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾, meaning: the people of Makkah. ﴿Nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾. Concerning its meaning there are several opinions:

One: This refers to a group of Muslims who remained in Makkah after the Messenger's hijrah, and Allah would not punish them while among them were those who sought forgiveness.

It is also said: It refers to a group from the people of Makkah whom Allah, may He be exalted, knew would believe and seek forgiveness, such as Abu Sufyan, Safwan ibn Umayyah, Ikrimah ibn Abi Jahl, Suhayl ibn Amr, Hakim ibn Hizam, and others like them. Since it was in Allah's knowledge that they would become among His companions, submitting and seeking forgiveness, He counted them among those seeking forgiveness at that moment.

It is also said that its meaning is: Allah would not punish them while among their loins was one who seeks forgiveness, since some of them had children who had embraced Islam.

It is also said: He only said ﴿Nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾ as an invitation for them to Islam and to seeking forgiveness, like a man who says: "I will not punish you while you obey me," meaning: obey me so that I will not punish you.

In a report: The Prophet (ﷺ) said: "Allah sent down to me two securities for my community: ﴿But Allah would not punish them while you are among them, nor would Allah punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾. When I die, I have left them the seeking of forgiveness until the Day of Resurrection." It is in the Jami' of Abu Isa through the route of Abu Musa al-Ash'ari.

And from Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, that he said: Whoever says every day: "I seek forgiveness from Allah, there is no god but He, the Living, the Self-Subsisting, and I turn to Him in repentance," three times, Allah will forgive his sins even if he fled from the battlefield.

From this narration, those who count fleeing from the battlefield among the major sins have derived their evidence.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 34:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And what is [the matter] with them that Allah should not punish them?﴾ If someone says: How is this reconciled with His words: ﴿And Allah would not punish them while you are among them﴾? It is said: By the first, He meant the punishment of annihilation (ʿadhab al-istiʾṣāl), and by this one, the punishment of the sword (ʿadhab al-sayf). It is also said: By the first He meant the punishment of this world, and by the second, the punishment of the Hereafter.

It is also said: What is meant is those whose punishment was withheld because the Prophet (ﷺ) was among them, and its meaning is: "And what is with them that Allah should not punish them after your departure from among them?"

﴿while they bar [people] from the Sacred Mosque﴾, that is, they prevent [people] from it. ﴿And they are not its guardians﴾. This is because they used to claim: "We are the guardians of the House." ﴿Its guardians are only the God-fearing﴾, meaning: the believers. ﴿But most of them do not know.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 35:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Their prayer at the House was nothing but whistling and clapping.﴾ Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, and al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with them, said: al-mukaa' is whistling, and al-tasdiyah is clapping. Linguistically, al-mukaa' is the name of a bird that has a whistle, so it is as if he said: "nothing but the sound of a mukaa'." Mujahid said: al-mukaa' is when one places his fingers in his cheeks, and al-tasdiyah is whistling; so he made the two into one thing. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: al-tasdiyah is their turning people away from the Sacred Mosque. The first view is more sound. The poet said:

(And the husband of a coquette, whom I left felled, whose ribcage whistles like the cheek of a one-eyed... )

That is: his ribcage whistles like the cheek of a one-eyed man (al-a'lam).

The story behind this is that four men from the clan of Banu 'Abd al-Dar would stand, when the Prophet (ﷺ) prayed in the Sacred Mosque: two stood on his right and two on his left. The two on his right would whistle and the two on his left would clap, so that they would confuse his recitation.

Ibn al-Anbari said: It was called a prayer only because they were commanded to pray in the mosque; when they placed that action in the place of prayer, it was called a prayer. ﴿So taste the punishment because you used to disbelieve.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 36:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to avert [people] from the way of Allah. They will spend it; then it will become a source of regret for them; then they will be overcome.﴾ Concerning this there are two opinions.

The first: the verse concerns the ones who fed [the army] (al-mut'imin) on the day of Badr. They were twelve men from the leaders of the polytheists: Abu Jahl ibn Hisham, al-Harith ibn Hisham, Ubayy ibn Khalaf, 'Utbah and Shaybah, the two sons of Rabi'ah, Munabbih and Nubayh, the two sons of al-Hajjaj, Abu al-Bukhturi ibn Hisham, Hakim ibn Hizam, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, Zam'ah ibn al-Aswad, and al-'Abbas ibn 'Abd al-Muttalib; because each one of them used to slaughter ten camels every day and feed the army.

The second opinion: this was revealed concerning Abu Sufyan ibn Harb, who hired three thousand men from the Ahabish on the day of Uhud to fight the Prophet (ﷺ). Then the words of the Exalted were revealed: ﴿Indeed, those who disbelieve spend their wealth to avert [people] from the way of Allah. Then it will be a source of regret for them on the Day of Resurrection; then they will be overcome.﴾

Al-Hasan said: The most intense regret on the Day of Resurrection belongs to the one who sees his wealth placed in the scale of another. ﴿And those who disbelieve will be gathered to Hell.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 37:

The Exalted's words: ﴿That Allah may distinguish the wicked from the good﴾. That is: that Allah may separate the wicked (al-khabith) from the good (al-tayyib). The wicked is what is spent from the unlawful (haram), and the good is what is spent from the lawful (halal). It has also been said: the wicked is what is spent in disobedience (ma'siyah), and the good is what is spent in obedience (ta'ah).

﴿And place the wicked, heaped one upon another, and put it all together﴾. That is: He gathers it all together. It is said: "a cloud is *markum*" when some of it is upon other parts of it. ﴿So He puts it into Hell. Those are the losers.﴾

And on the authority of 'Ubadah ibn al-Samit, may Allah be pleased with him, who said: Allah, the Exalted, will gather the world on the Day of Resurrection, and He will take what belongs to Him and cast the rest into the Fire. And for what purpose does He cast it into the Fire? It has been said: to constrict the place for the disbelievers; and it has been said: so that the regret will be more severe for them when they look upon it.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 38:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Say to those who disbelieve: if they cease, what has passed will be forgiven them﴾. Yahya ibn Mu'adh al-Razi, may Allah have mercy on him, said: "Faith that is not too weak to demolish the disbelief that preceded it—when would it be too weak to demolish a sin that follows it?"

﴿And if they return, then the way of the former peoples has already passed﴾. It was said: the way of the former peoples is that worldly punishment is followed by the punishment of the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verses 39–40:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah (persecution/disbelief), and the religion is entirely for Allah.﴾ That is: there should be no shirk (associating partners with Allah). ﴿But if they cease, then indeed Allah is Seeing of what they do. And if they turn away, then know that Allah is your Protector; an excellent Protector and an excellent Helper.﴾ As for al-Mawla (the Protector): it is the one who manages affairs; and an-Nasir (the Helper): it is the one who gives victory.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verses 39–40:

The words of the Exalted: ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah (persecution/disbelief), and the religion is entirely for Allah.﴾ That is: there should be no shirk (associating partners with Allah). ﴿But if they cease, then indeed Allah is Seeing of what they do. And if they turn away, then know that Allah is your Protector; an excellent Protector and an excellent Helper.﴾ As for al-Mawla (the Protector): it is the one who manages affairs; and an-Nasir (the Helper): it is the one who gives victory.

The statement of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿And know that whatever you acquire as spoils of war, a fifth of it belongs to Allah and to the Messenger﴾ ... the verse.

The scholars differed regarding the *ghanimah* (spoils of war taken by force) and the *fay'* (property acquired without battle). One view is that they are the same, namely property taken from the disbelievers by force.

The second view, which is the more sound (*al-asahh*), is that they differ. The distinction is that the *ghanimah* is property taken from the disbelievers by force, through the pressing of horses and riding animals, while the *fay'* is property taken without the pressing of horses or riding animals.

This view is transmitted from Sufyan al-Thawri and al-Shafi'i, may Allah be pleased with them both, and others.

﴿Then for Allah...﴾ Most exegetes hold that His saying ﴿for Allah﴾ is an introductory phrase (*iftitah kalam*), and that Allah has no separate share. Rather, Allah's share and the Messenger's share are one.

There is another view: that Allah has a share which is spent on the Ka'bah. It is narrated that al-Hasan ibn Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyyah was asked about this verse, and he said: "His saying ﴿Then for Allah is its fifth﴾ is an introductory phrase; to Allah belongs this world and the next." It is also narrated from Abu al-'Aliyah al-Riyahi who said: "The Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) would divide the spoils into five shares, then set aside the fifth from it. Then he would take from it a handful and assign it to the Ka'bah, and then divide the rest according to what Allah has mentioned."

As for His saying ﴿and to the Messenger﴾, most exegetes hold that the Messenger has a separate share. Some said that the Messenger has no share at all; rather, it is an introductory phrase, and the mention of the Messenger means that the management of it belongs to him.

Then they differed, according to the first view, as to who receives that share after his death.

Qatadah said: it belongs to the caliph after him. Some said: it is returned to the four shares. As for the school of al-Shafi'i, that share is spent on the public interests (*al-masalih*).

There is a fourth view: that it is spent on horses and weapons in the way of Allah. This is narrated from Ibrahim al-Nakha'i and others.

As for His saying ﴿and to the near of kin﴾ (*dhi al-qurba*), they differed on this in three opinions:

The school of al-Shafi'i holds that they have a separate share after the Messenger of Allah until the Hour, shared by their rich and poor alike, according to what is well known. This is also the view of Ahmad and others.

Malik said: the matter is left to the imam; if he wishes he gives them, and if he wishes he does not give them. The same applies to the remaining shares. They were mentioned only to permit giving to them, not as an entitlement.

The second view, which is the school of Abu Hanifah, may Allah be pleased with him: the share of the near of kin is returned to the rest, and they have no separate share. It is divided into three shares: for orphans, the needy and the wayfarer. They narrate that the four caliphs divided it in this manner, and Allah knows best what is correct.

Then they differed as to who the near of kin are. Mujahid said: they are the Banu Hashim specifically. It is narrated from Ibn 'Abbas that he said: they are all of Quraysh. It is also related that he was asked about the share of the near of kin, and he said: "We claim that it is for us, but our people refuse this for us."

﴿and the needy and the wayfarer, if you have believed in Allah and in what We sent down upon Our servant on the Day of Criterion, the day the two hosts met﴾

The third view: the near of kin are the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib. This is the view of al-Shafi'i, may Allah have mercy on him, and it is indicated by the report transmitted through Jubayr ibn Mut'im, may Allah be pleased with him, from the Prophet: "He divided the share of the near of kin between the Banu Hashim and the Banu al-Muttalib. I and 'Uthman walked to the Messenger of Allah and said: 'O Messenger of Allah, we do not deny the virtue of the Banu Hashim, because of your position which Allah placed among them. But we and our brothers the Banu al-Muttalib are equal in kinship to you. You have given to them and deprived us.' He said: 'I and the Banu al-Muttalib are one thing,' and he interlaced his fingers between each other, 'and they never separated from us in the Jahiliyyah or in Islam.'"

As for His saying the Exalted ﴿and the orphans﴾: the orphans have a separate share by way of support. The orphan who deserves the share is the one who has no father, so that he is young and poor.

His saying ﴿and the needy﴾: the needy (*al-masakin*) are the people of need. The difference between the *miskin* and the *faqir* will come in Surat Bara'ah.

As for His saying ﴿and the wayfarer﴾: he is the one cut off from his wealth, having been separated from it.

His saying ﴿if you have believed in Allah﴾ means: "Know that whatever you acquire as spoils of war, a fifth of it belongs to Allah and to the Messenger, as has been mentioned, if you have believed in Allah." It was also said that its meaning is: "They both command regarding it what they will, so accept it, if you have believed in Allah."

His saying the Exalted ﴿and what We sent down﴾ means: if you have believed in Allah and in what We sent down ﴿upon Our servant﴾.

There is another view: that this refers back to His saying the Exalted: ﴿And fight them until there is no more fitnah﴾, [on the condition] that you have believed in Allah and in what We sent down upon Our servant ﴿on the Day of Criterion﴾, the Day of Badr, on which Allah the Exalted distinguished between truth and falsehood, ﴿the day the two hosts met﴾, meaning: the party of Allah met the party of Satan. ﴿And Allah is competent over all things﴾.

It is narrated from al-Sha'bi that he said: "The Day of Criterion was the seventeenth day of Ramadan, when Allah the Exalted announced the completeness of His power."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 42:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿When you were on the nearer side of the valley﴾ to the end of the verse. Al-'Adwah (the edge, or bank) of the valley is its brink; al-ghadwah and al-'adwah are one and the same. His saying ﴿al-dunya﴾ means the nearer to Madinah, so it is the feminine of al-adna (the nearer). ﴿And they were on the farther side﴾ means the farther from Makkah, and it is the feminine of al-aqsa (the farthest). ﴿And the caravan was below you﴾: they said its meaning is that the caravan was at a place lower than you. Al-rakb (the caravan) is the convoy on which Abu Sufyan was, and they were on the coast of the sea, three miles from Badr. ﴿And even if you had made an appointment together, you would have differed concerning the appointment﴾: its meaning is that even if you had agreed upon a meeting and gathering for battle, you would have differed, because of your fewness and their multitude. ﴿Concerning the appointment; but [Allah brought you together] without an appointment﴾, and Allah gathered you without any appointment, ﴿that Allah might accomplish a matter that was [destined to be] done﴾.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That those who perish might perish upon clear evidence﴾ to the end of the verse. In it there are two views:

The first, which is the more apparent, is that destruction (al-halak) is disbelief and life (al-hayah) is faith. Its meaning: that whoever disbelieves might disbelieve after a clear proof, concerning what is for him and against him. ﴿And he who lives might live upon evidence﴾, meaning: and whoever believes might believe upon the like of that.

The second view: destruction is death and life is living. Its meaning: that whoever dies might die after a clear proof, and whoever lives might live upon the like of that.

﴿And indeed, Allah is Hearing and Knowing﴾: Hearing of your statements, Knowing of your affairs.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 43:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿When God showed them to you in your dream as few﴾ and the rest of the verse. There are two opinions concerning it.

The more apparent of the two opinions is that the manam (dream, i.e. sleep) is literally sleep; so the Messenger of God saw them in his sleep as fewer in number than they actually were.

The second opinion, which is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri, is that His saying ﴿in your dream﴾ means: in your eye, as few. He called the eye a manam (dream) because it is the place of sleep.

﴿And if He had shown them to you as many, you would have lost heart﴾ meaning: you would have become cowardly, ﴿and you would have disputed about the matter﴾ meaning: concerning advancing or holding back. ﴿But God saved you﴾ meaning: He preserved you from failure and cowardice. ﴿Indeed, He is Knowing of what is in the breasts﴾.

It is established from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he used to seek refuge with God from cowardice.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 44:

Allah the Exalted's saying: ﴿And when He showed them to you, when you met, as few in your eyes, and made you appear few in their eyes, that Allah might accomplish a matter already decreed; and to Allah are returned all matters.﴾ The meaning of the verse: Allah the Exalted made the polytheists appear few in the eyes of the believers, so that they would advance and not lose heart; and He made the believers appear few in the eyes of the disbelievers, so that they would not flee.

It is narrated from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud that he said: On the day of Badr I said to some of those beside me: "I see them as seventy men." He said: "I see them as a hundred." Then we took some of them as prisoners and we asked them: "How many were you?" They said: "We were a thousand." ﴿That Allah might accomplish﴾, meaning: that Allah might accomplish the exaltation of Islam, the humiliation of polytheism, the victory of the believers, and the killing of the polytheists.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 45:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿O you who believe, when you encounter a company (fiʼah), stand firm⁠—﴾ and so on. The fiʼah (fiʼa) means a group, a company.

His saying: ﴿So stand firm and remember Allah much, that you may be successful.﴾ The meaning of remembering Allah is supplication for victory and triumph. ﴿That you may be successful⁠—﴾ and be hopeful of success.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 46:

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And obey Allah and His Messenger﴾ and so on. As for His words: ﴿and do not dispute, lest you lose heart﴾, its meaning is: do not differ, lest you become weak. ﴿And your strength will depart﴾: its meaning is your might and your effort.

Qatadah said: "The wind (rih) here means the wind of victory." It is authentically reported from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said: "I was given victory by the east wind (al-saba), and the people of 'Ad were destroyed by the west wind (al-dabur)."

The third opinion, that of al-Akhfash and others: ﴿and your strength will depart﴾ means your dominion (dawlah). ﴿And be patient; indeed, Allah is with the patient﴾: its interpretation is well known.

In this verse there is a great virtue for those who are patient, for Allah the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, Allah is with the patient.﴾ The poet said:

(Indeed I have seen in the days a trial / for patience, a praiseworthy outcome and effect.)

The words of Allah the Exalted: ﴿And do not be like those who went out from their homes in insolence and to be seen by people﴾ and so on. Al-batar: transgression in blessings and abandoning gratitude. Al-riya': displaying what is beautiful and concealing what is ugly.

The verse was revealed about the polytheists when they came toward Badr,

Then God, exalted is He, said to the believers: ﴿And do not be like those who went out from their homes insolently and to be seen by people﴾.

﴿And [they] hinder [others] from the way of God﴾: its meaning is that they prevent [people] from the way of truth. ﴿And God is encompassing of what they do﴾. It is narrated from the Prophet (ﷺ) that he said when the polytheists approached: "O God, this is Quraysh, coming with their pride and their arrogance, opposing You and opposing Your Messenger." The report continues to its end.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 48:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And [remember] when Satan made their deeds appear pleasing to them and said, "No one among the people can overcome you today, and indeed, I am your protector."﴾ The verse... It is related that Iblis, may he receive what he deserves, took the form of Suraqah ibn Malik and said to the polytheists: ﴿And indeed, I am your protector,﴾ meaning: a protector for you against the Banu Kinanah, so that no harm from them will befall you. Then he began inciting them to fight. ﴿And when the two hosts sighted each other﴾ meaning: the two groups met, the believers and the polytheists. ﴿He turned back on his heels﴾ meaning: he retreated backward on his heels. ﴿And said, "Indeed, I am free of you."﴾ In the account: he was holding the hand of al-Harith ibn Hisham, the brother of Abu Jahl. When he saw the angels descending from the sky, led by Jibril (peace be upon him), he pulled his hand out of al-Harith's hand and fled. Al-Harith said to him, "Are you fleeing without fighting?" and began to hold him, but he pushed him in the chest and said: ﴿Indeed, I see what you do not see,﴾ and fled. ﴿Indeed, I fear Allah.﴾

If someone says: How could he say "Indeed, I fear Allah" when he refused to prostrate to Adam, and he did not fear Allah? The answer to this has two opinions:

One of them: he said this as a lie. The second opinion: he feared that he would be seized and disgraced among mankind. Some of them said: he feared that his term had come. ﴿And Allah is severe in punishment.﴾

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 49:

The Exalted's saying: ﴿When the hypocrites and those in whose hearts is a disease say, "These have been deluded by their religion."﴾ These were a people who had embraced Islam in Makkah but had not emigrated. Some doubt remained in their hearts, so they went out with the polytheists, and they said, "If we see that Muhammad has strength, we will join him." When they saw the scarcity of the believers and the weakness of their power, they said this statement, so Allah the Exalted revealed this verse: ﴿When the hypocrites say...﴾ the verse.

The Exalted's saying: ﴿And whoever relies upon Allah﴾, whoever trusts in Allah, ﴿then indeed, Allah is Almighty, All-Wise.﴾ We have already explained the meaning of al-Aziz (the Almighty) and al-Hakim (the All-Wise) earlier.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 50:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if you could see when the angels take the souls of those who disbelieve﴾, concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: this refers to the moment of death, and His saying ﴿they strike their faces and their backs﴾ means they strike their faces with whips of fire, and their backs, driving them toward the punishment.

The second opinion: the taking (tawaffi) here is killing, meaning: the angels killed the polytheists at Badr. His saying ﴿they strike their faces and their backs﴾ means: they strike them with the sword when they advance. And His saying ﴿and their backs﴾ means they strike them with the sword when they turn away, and they say: ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning﴾.

It is related from al-Hasan al-Basri that he said: With the angels are maqami' (iron rods) of iron with which they strike the disbelievers, so the fire flares up in their wounds; this is the meaning of His saying: ﴿Taste the punishment of the burning﴾.
The saying of Allah, the Exalted: ﴿That is because of what your hands have sent forward, and because Allah is not unjust to the servants.﴾ Its meaning is clear.

Almighty Allah's saying: ﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh﴾ up to the end of the verse. Here "al-da'b" (custom, habit) carries the meaning of "al-ʿādah," and its meaning is: their habit in disbelief was like the habit of the people of Pharaoh. ﴿And those before them disbelieved in the signs of Allah﴾ up to the end of the verse. The meaning of the verse is clear.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 53:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿That is because Allah never changed a favour He had bestowed upon a people﴾ to the end of the verse. Concerning this there are two opinions:

The first: its meaning is ﴿He never changed a favour﴾, that is, He never replaced the blessing with affliction, ﴿until they change what is in themselves﴾, that is, until they abandon gratitude and adopt ingratitude (kufran).

The second opinion: this refers to the people of Makkah. The Messenger was a favour that Allah, exalted is He, had bestowed upon them, but they disbelieved in this favour, so Allah, exalted is He, changed it. Its meaning is that He transferred it to the people of Madinah. ﴿And that Allah is All-Hearing, All-Knowing﴾, meaning, they are both known.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 54:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿Like the custom of the people of Pharaoh﴾. Its meaning is: as we have explained (previously). The repetition of the mention is for emphasis. It is also possible that this (ruin) occurred to other peoples besides the first ones.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those before them denied the signs of their Lord, so We destroyed them for their sins﴾. He means: We destroy these people just as We destroyed those.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And We drowned the people of Pharaoh, and all of them were wrongdoers﴾. He means: the earlier and the later ones.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 55:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the worst of living creatures in the sight of Allah are those who disbelieve﴾, to the end of the verse. This verse is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿They are like cattle; rather, they are further astray﴾. Allah, exalted is He, named them "living creatures" (dawabb) and "cattle" (an'am), because of how little they benefit from their intellects (uqul), their minds (albab), their hearing and their sight. ﴿So they do not believe﴾; its meaning is clear.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 56:

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Those with whom you made a treaty among them﴾. This verse was revealed concerning a group of the polytheists who made a covenant with the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ), then broke the covenant. So Allah, exalted is He, said: ﴿Those with whom you made a treaty among them, then they break their covenant every time﴾, meaning: whenever they made a covenant, they broke it. ﴿And they do not fear (Allah)﴾, meaning: they do not fear breaking the covenant.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 57:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿If you encounter them in war﴾ means: if you come upon them in war. ﴿Then make an example of them for those behind them﴾. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: "Warn those behind them through them." The poet said:

(I go about the valleys every day, fearing that the wise one may make an example of me)

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿so that they may take heed﴾ means: so that they may remember.

The meaning of the verse: We should inflict such punishment upon those who came to fight you, or who broke their covenant with you, that it scatters those behind them of their groups.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 58:

So His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And if you fear treachery from a people﴾ — the verse. The meaning of "fear" (al-mukhafah) here is: the perception of treachery.

﴿Then throw back to them [their covenant] on equal terms﴾ — meaning: throw back the covenant to them ﴿on equal terms﴾, meaning: in a state where you and they are equal in knowledge of it.

The intended meaning of the verse is: do not fight them before you have cancelled the covenant and before they know of the cancellation, so that you are not ascribed to breaking the covenant. This verse is counted among the eloquent verses of the Qur'an.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, Allah does not love the treacherous﴾ — and its meaning is known.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 59:

The words of the Most High (﴿And let not those who disbelieve suppose that they have outstripped [Us]﴾) and the rest of the verse concern the polytheists who fled on the day of Badr. His words ﴿outstripped﴾ mean: escaped.

His words ﴿Indeed, they cannot escape﴾ mean: they cannot get away from Me. Ibn Muhaysin recited it as "لايعجزون" (la yu'jizun, read as one word), but the correct reading is the first. The verse has been recited with two readings: "أنهم" (annahum) and "إنهم" (innahum). So His words "إنهم" (innahum) are in the manner of a new sentence beginning, while His words "أنهم" (annahum) mean: because they cannot escape. The meaning of "fawat" (escape, failing to be caught) is transmitted from Abu 'Ubayda, and from al-Hasan al-Basri who said: ﴿they cannot escape﴾ means: even if the punishment of this world escapes them, they will not escape the punishment of the Hereafter.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 60:

And His, the Exalted's, saying: ﴿And prepare against them whatever you can of power and of steeds of war (ribat al-khayl)﴾ — the verse. I'd (al-i'dad, preparation) is taking something for the time of need. And His saying: ﴿of power﴾ has several opinions. ﴿By which you may strike terror into the enemy of Allah and your enemy, and others besides them whom you do not know, [but] Allah knows them. And whatever you spend in the way of Allah will be fully repaid to you, and you will not be wronged.﴾

The first: what 'Uqbah ibn 'Amir reported: "The Prophet recited this verse on the pulpit, then said: 'Indeed, the power is archery. Indeed, the power is archery.'" Muslim included it in his Sahih.

The second opinion: that the power refers to male horses, and ribat refers to female horses. This is the view of 'Ikrimah.

It is also related from Khalid ibn al-Walid that he would not ride in battle except female horses, because of the scarcity of their neighing.

And from Abu Muhayriz, who said: "They used to prefer riding male horses when lining up in ranks, and riding female horses during stationing and raids."

The third opinion: that power is all weaponry. It has also been said: power is fortresses, and fortresses are horses. The poet said:

(And indeed I have known, despite my avoidance of destruction, that fortresses are horses, not the clay of the villages.)

His saying: ﴿By which you may strike terror﴾ means: you frighten by it ﴿the enemy of Allah and your enemy﴾, i.e., the enemies of Allah and your enemies, "enemy" being singular with the sense of plural. His saying: ﴿and others besides them﴾ means: you strike terror by it into others besides them, and they differed about its meaning:

It is related from Mujahid that he said: they are the Banu Qurayzah. There is another opinion regarding it: that they are the hypocrites.

And there is a third opinion: that they are the jinn. And from al-Suddi, who said: the people of Persia.

It is related from the Prophet that he said: "Jinn will not afflict a human in whose house there is a noble horse." Al-Naqqash included it in his tafsir.

And regarding the verse there is a fourth opinion: it is related from Mu'adh ibn Jabal that he said: ﴿and others besides them﴾ refers to the devils.

His saying: ﴿whom you do not know, [but] Allah knows them﴾ is clear.

His saying: ﴿And whatever you spend in the way of Allah will be fully repaid to you, and you will not be wronged﴾ means: your rewards will not be diminished.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 61:

Allah's words: ﴿And if they incline to peace, then incline to it﴾. As-Salm, as-Silm and as-Salm (السّلم وَالسّلم وَالسّلم) mean reconciliation (al-sulh), and the meaning is: if they lean toward reconciliation, then you lean toward it as well.

It is narrated from al-Hasan and Qatadah that they both said: this verse is abrogated (mansukhah) by the verse of the sword.

Allah's words: ﴿And put your trust in Allah﴾. Its meaning: have confidence in Allah. ﴿Indeed, He is the All-Hearing, the All-Knowing﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 62:

Allah the Exalted's words: ﴿And if they intend to deceive you﴾. Al-khada' (deception) is: that one shows the opposite of what one conceals.

His words: ﴿then indeed Allah is sufficient for you﴾, meaning: then indeed Allah is your sufficiency (kafi). ﴿It is He who supported you with His help﴾: it is He who strengthened you with His help. ﴿And with the believers﴾: that is, He strengthened you with the believers.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 63:

﴿And He joined their hearts together.﴾ Most of the exegetes (mufassirun) say that this refers to the Aws and the Khazraj. There had been enmities (ihn) and grudges (tarath) between them in the pre-Islamic era (al-Jahiliyya), and fighting between them had persisted for a hundred years. So God joined their hearts together through the Prophet. Al-Zajjaj said: A man among them would slap another, and he would fight with his strength until he gained satisfaction from it. Then God joined their hearts together through Islam, until a man would fight his brother and his relative on account of Islam.

It is narrated from Ibn Mas'ud (may Allah be pleased with him) that he said: The verse was revealed concerning those who love one another for the sake of God.

In the reports (akhbar) from the Prophet (ﷺ) it is said: "The believer is one who is affectionate (ma'lafa), and there is no good in one who neither befriends nor is befriended."

It is narrated from Khalid ibn Ma'dan that he said: Indeed, God has an angel in the heaven, half of whom is of snow and half of whom is of fire, and his glorification is: "O God, just as You have joined snow and fire together, join together the hearts of Your righteous servants."

As for His saying ﴿Even if you had spent all that is on the earth, you could not have joined their hearts, but God joined them together. Indeed, He is Exalted in Might, Wise.﴾ That is: Invincible in His dominion (mani' fi mulkih), Wise in His creation (hakim fi khalqih).

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 64:

The words of the Most High: ﴿O Prophet, Allah is sufficient for you, and for those believers who follow you﴾. It is related from Ibn ʿAbbas, by the narration of al-Walibi, that he said: Thirty-nine men and twenty-three women embraced Islam, and then ʿUmar (raḍiya Allahu ʿanhu) embraced Islam, completing the forty. So Allah the Most High revealed this verse.

Regarding the verse there are two opinions. The first: ﴿O Prophet, Allah is sufficient for you, and for those who follow you﴾, meaning: Allah suffices you and suffices those believers who follow you. In this case, "man" (min, "those who") is in the accusative position (manṣūb).

The second opinion: ﴿Allah is sufficient for you﴾, and "sufficient for you" refers to your followers among the believers. In this case, "man" (min, "those who") is in the nominative position (marfūʿ). The poet said:

(When the battle rages and the staves are broken, then sufficient for you is al-Ḍaḥḥak, a keen sword.)

This is cited as evidence for the first opinion.

And al-Shaʿbi read: "Ḥasbuka Allahu wa man ittabaʿaka min al-mu'minin" (Allah is sufficient for you, and so are those believers who follow you), and its meaning is close to the first.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 65:

The Most High's words: ﴿O Prophet, urge the believers to fight﴾ It is reported in the irregular reading (shadhdh): "ḥaraṣ al-mu'minīn" with an unpointed ṣād (ṣ), whereas the well-known reading is with a pointed ḍād (ḍ). And al-taḥrīḍ (urging) is: urging someone to hasten toward a thing.

The Most High's words: ﴿If there are twenty of you who are steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are a hundred of you, they will overcome a thousand of those who disbelieve﴾ This is a report with the meaning of a command. Allah the Most High had commanded the believers that one of them should not flee from ten, and that a hundred of them should not flee from a thousand. If someone says: What is the meaning of ﴿because they are a people who do not understand﴾, and what is its connection to the meaning of the verse?

Its answer: its meaning is that they fight out of ignorance, not out of reckoning and insight, whereas you fight out of insight and reckoning. Thus they will not stand firm when you stand firm. Then the Muslims asked Allah for lightening, and Allah the Most High revealed the other verse, and commanded that one should not flee from two, and a hundred from two hundred.

If someone says: Allah the Most High said: ﴿they will overcome two hundred﴾, and we have seen fighting against this number without overcoming, so how does the meaning of the verse stand, and failure in the report of Allah is not permissible?

We say: the meaning of His words ﴿they will overcome﴾ is "they will fight"; as if He commanded them to fight in hope of victory and support from Allah the Most High.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 66:

As for His saying, ﴿Now Allah has lightened your burden﴾, this verse abrogates (nāsikh, the verse that cancels a prior ruling; naskh) the first verse. Abu Ja'far Yazid ibn al-Qa'qa' recited: "wa-'alima anna fikum du'afa'" (and He knew that among you there are weak ones), whereas the well-known reading is "du'afa'" and "du'afan," and both have the same meaning.

﴿If there are among you a hundred steadfast, they will overcome two hundred; and if there are among you a thousand, they will overcome two thousand, by the permission of Allah. And Allah is with the steadfast.﴾ The rest of the verse is clear in meaning.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 67:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿It is not for a Prophet to have captives﴾. It is read as "asra" and "asara". The scholars of the language (ahl al-lughah) said: asra is the plural of asir (captive), and asara is the plural of the plural. al-Asma'i related from Abu 'Amr ibn al-'Ala' that he said: "The asra are those taken without being bound, and the asara are those who were taken and bound." The more correct view among the scholars of the language is that there is no difference between them, as related by al-Azhari.

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿until he has inflicted a massacre upon the land﴾. al-Ithkhan (massacre, mass slaughter): killing. It was also said: going to great lengths in subduing and punishing.

﴿You desire the goods of this world﴾ by means of ransom (al-ifda').

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿but Allah desires the Hereafter﴾. Its meaning: He encourages you towards the Hereafter. As for His saying: ﴿And Allah is Mighty and Wise﴾, we have already mentioned the meaning of al-'Aziz (the Mighty) and al-Hakim (the Wise).

Know that this verse was revealed concerning the captives of Badr. It has been narrated that the Prophet (ﷺ) killed seventy on the day of Badr and took seventy of the polytheists captive. Then he consulted his companions about the captives. Abu Bakr (may Allah be pleased with him) said: "These are your people, your kin and your family. Spare them, perhaps Allah will guide them through you, and take ransom from them, so that it becomes a support for the Muslims." 'Umar said: "These have harmed you, expelled you, and disbelieved in what you brought. So strike their necks." The Messenger inclined to the opinion of Abu Bakr and preferred what he had said.

It has been narrated that he said to Abu Bakr: "Your likeness is that of Abraham when he said: ﴿Whoever follows me is of me, and whoever disobeys me, then You are Forgiving and Merciful﴾," and he said to 'Umar: "Your likeness is that of Noah when he said: ﴿My Lord, do not leave upon the earth any of the disbelievers as a dweller﴾." Then he said to his companions: "None of you should be left with a captive except by ransom or by striking his neck." So they took ransom, and the ransom for each captive was forty ounces, an ounce being forty dirhams. Then Allah, may He be exalted, revealed this verse to its end.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verses 68–69:

The words of God Most High: ﴿Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had already gone forth, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took﴾. It is related from the Prophet, through the transmission of Abu Hurayrah, that he said: "Spoils of war were not made lawful for any black-headed people before you; a fire used to descend from the sky and consume them." Abu Hurayrah said: "When the day of Badr came and they fell into what they fell into of the spoils, and they ransomed the captives before the revelation permitting this had descended, Allah Most High revealed: ﴿Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had already gone forth, a great punishment would have touched you﴾ to the end of the verse." There are several opinions concerning the meaning of the verse:

The first: Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had already gone forth concerning the permissibility of the spoils, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and a group.

The second: Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had already gone forth regarding His forgiveness of the people of Badr for what they did, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took. This is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri.

The third: Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had already gone forth that they would not be sent a prior prohibition against taking [spoils], a great punishment would have touched you for what you took, for He does not punish without a prior warning.

It is authentically related from the Prophet that he said: "I was shown your punishment [that would have come] short of this tree," and he pointed to a tree near him. It is also related that he said to Umar: "Had the punishment descended, none would have been saved except you." And it is related that he said to him: "It nearly struck us."

It is also related that when the first verse was revealed, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah withheld their hands from what they had taken as ransom, so Allah Most High revealed this verse to its end.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verses 68–69:

The words of God Most High: ﴿Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had already gone forth, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took﴾. It is related from the Prophet, through the transmission of Abu Hurayrah, that he said: "Spoils of war were not made lawful for any black-headed people before you; a fire used to descend from the sky and consume them." Abu Hurayrah said: "When the day of Badr came and they fell into what they fell into of the spoils, and they ransomed the captives before the revelation permitting this had descended, Allah Most High revealed: ﴿Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had already gone forth, a great punishment would have touched you﴾ to the end of the verse." There are several opinions concerning the meaning of the verse:

The first: Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had already gone forth concerning the permissibility of the spoils, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took. This is the view of Sa'id ibn Jubayr and a group.

The second: Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had already gone forth regarding His forgiveness of the people of Badr for what they did, a great punishment would have touched you for what you took. This is the view of al-Hasan al-Basri.

The third: Had it not been for a decree from Allah that had already gone forth that they would not be sent a prior prohibition against taking [spoils], a great punishment would have touched you for what you took, for He does not punish without a prior warning.

It is authentically related from the Prophet that he said: "I was shown your punishment [that would have come] short of this tree," and he pointed to a tree near him. It is also related that he said to Umar: "Had the punishment descended, none would have been saved except you." And it is related that he said to him: "It nearly struck us."

It is also related that when the first verse was revealed, the Companions of the Messenger of Allah withheld their hands from what they had taken as ransom, so Allah Most High revealed this verse to its end.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿O Prophet, say to those prisoners who are in your hands﴾. This verse was revealed concerning al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib, for he was taken captive on the day of Badr, and with him were twenty ounces of gold, which were taken from him. Then the Prophet (ﷺ) said to him: "Ransom yourself and your two nephews — meaning ʿAqil and Nawfal." He said: "I have no property; you have already taken what I had." He said: "Where is the wealth that you handed over to Umm al-Fadl, and said: 'If I am struck in this venture, then for ʿAbd Allah such-and-such, and for al-Fadl such-and-such, and for Quthm such-and-such'?" He said: "By God, no one was with us. So I bear witness that there is no god but God and that you are the Messenger of God." Then he ransomed himself and his two nephews, and God the Exalted revealed this verse to its end.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿If God knows any good in your hearts﴾. Its meaning: if God knows faith in your hearts.

The words of the Exalted: ﴿He will give you better than what was taken from you﴾. Al-ʿAbbas said: "God has indeed given me better than what was taken from me, for he had twenty slaves, each of whom trades with twenty thousand dirhams."

And His words: ﴿And He will forgive you, and God is Forgiving and Merciful﴾. Al-ʿAbbas said: "And I hope for forgiveness from God."

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 71:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And if they intend treachery against you﴾. Al-khiyanah (treachery) is the opposite of al-amanah (trustworthiness). Its meaning: if they intend to disbelieve in you. ﴿Then they have betrayed Allah before⦆ i.e., they have disbelieved in Allah before.

His saying: ﴿So He gave you power over them﴾, meaning: He gave you power over them. ﴿And Allah is Knowing, Wise﴾.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 72:

Allah's statement: ﴿Indeed, those who believed and emigrated and strove with their wealth and their lives in the cause of Allah﴾ – the verse... The hijrah (emigration, departure from one's homeland to another land) was obligatory at the beginning of Islam. Then, on the day of the conquest of Makkah, the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is no hijrah after today."

It is narrated from al-Hasan al-Basri that he said: The hijrah remains in effect until the Hour is established, so for the people of the desert (al-bawadi), when they accept Islam, it is incumbent upon them to emigrate to the cities (al-amsar).

His statement: ﴿And those who gave shelter and helped﴾ – these are the people of Madinah. The meaning of "giving shelter" (al-iwa') is that they took the emigrants (al-muhajirin) into their own homes and possessions, in their wealth and their dwellings.

His statement: ﴿They are allies of one another﴾ – concerning this there are two opinions:

One of them: they are helpers of one another.

The second opinion: its meaning is that they inherit from one another.

His statement, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who believed but did not emigrate – you have no obligation of protection toward them until they emigrate﴾ – the guardianship (muwalah) between the Muslims and them is severed until they emigrate. The emigrant would not inherit from the Bedouin (al-a'rabi), nor the Bedouin from the emigrant. Then He said: ﴿And if they seek your help in religion, then upon you is help﴾ – meaning: if those who did not emigrate seek your help, then you must help them. Then He made an exception and said: ﴿Except against a people between you and whom there is a covenant﴾ – i.e., a truce (muwada'ah), so do not help them against those people. His statement: ﴿And Allah is Seeing of what you do﴾ – its meaning is clear.

The Qur'anic phrase and commentary of al-Sam'ani on surah 8, verse 73:

His saying, may He be exalted: ﴿And those who disbelieve, some of them are allies of others﴾. He means: some of them are helpers of others.

The second opinion: some of them inherit from others.

And His saying ﴿Unless you do it﴾ means: if you do not accept this ruling, ﴿there will be turmoil in the land and great corruption﴾. The turmoil in the land: the strength of disbelief. And the great corruption: the weakness of faith.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 74:

The Almighty's saying: ﴿And those who believed and emigrated and strove in the way of Allah, and those who sheltered and helped⁠—﴾ (the verse). If it is said: what is the meaning of the repetition here?

We say: The emigrants were of several ranks. Some of them were of the first emigration (hijra), namely those who emigrated before Hudaybiyya, and some were of the second emigration, namely those who emigrated after Hudaybiyya and before the Conquest of Mecca. Some of them had two emigrations: the emigration to Abyssinia (al-Habasha) and the emigration to Medina. So the intended meaning of the first verse is the first emigration, and the intended meaning of the second is the second emigration.

The Almighty's saying: ﴿Those are the true believers.﴾ It means: there is no doubt and no uncertainty concerning their faith.

His saying: ﴿For them is forgiveness and a generous provision.﴾ It has been related concerning the "generous provision" that it means the provision of Paradise, which does not become excrement, but rather becomes sweat, having the scent of musk.

Commentary of al-Sam'ani (Tafsir al-Quran) on surah 8, verse 75:

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And those who believed after [that] and emigrated and strove alongside you — they are of you﴾, to the end of the verse. He means by it: "they are with you, so you are of them and they are of you."

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿But blood relatives are closer to one another in the Book of Allah﴾. Most of the exegetes (mufassirun) hold that this verse abrogates (naskh) what preceded it concerning the establishment of inheritance through emigration, so inheritance was transferred from emigration to inheritance through kinship.

Allah the Exalted says: ﴿in the Book of Allah﴾, meaning: in the ruling of Allah.

As for His saying: ﴿Indeed, Allah is Knowing of all things﴾, the people of knowledge said: The intended meaning of "those of blood relationship" (ulu al-arham) is not the relatives who have neither agnatic claim (ta'sib) nor a fixed share (fard). Rather, the intended meaning of ulu al-arham is [the members of the agnatic groups] (ahl al-'asabat). Then the inheritance of relatives is mentioned in another place, which is the verse of inheritance. And Allah knows best.
